title: String Basics
intro: A **string** is text: a sequence of characters inside quotes. Single `'…'` and double `"…"` quotes both work. Each character has a position (an **index**) starting at **0**, and `len()` counts the characters.

questions.prompt: Use square brackets to read one character; negative indexes count from the end. `+` joins strings and `*` repeats them.
questions.exampleCode:
city = "Porto"
print(city[0], city[-1], len(city))
print(city + "!")
print("ha" * 3)
questions.explanation: `city[0]` is the first character and `city[-1]` the last. Spaces and punctuation count as characters too.

questions.prompt: `word` already holds a word. Store its first character in `first` and its last character in `last`.

tests.name: first
tests.code: assert first == word[0], 'first should be the character at index 0.'
tests.message: first should be the first character.

tests.name: last
tests.code: assert last == word[-1], 'last should be the final character — try a negative index.'
tests.message: last should be the last character.

questions.hint: Indexes start at 0. `-1` means the last one.
questions.explanation: Negative indexes save you from working out `len(word) - 1`.

questions.hint: `*` happens before `+`, just like in maths.

questions.prompt: `team` holds a team name. Store in `chant` the text `Go ` three times followed by the team — for example `Go Go Go Falcons`. Use `*` and `+`.

tests.name: chant
tests.code: assert chant == 'Go Go Go ' + team, 'chant should be "Go " three times, then the team name.'
tests.message: chant should be Go Go Go, then the team.

questions.hint: Repeat `"Go "` (with its space) three times, then add `team`.
questions.explanation: Building text from pieces with `*` and `+` keeps it correct for any team name.

questions.hint: Count every character, including the space.
questions.explanation: There are 11 letters plus 1 space, so the length is 12.

questions.prompt: This should store the text `It's raining`, but Python reports a *SyntaxError*. Fix it.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert message == "It's raining", 'message should be: It\'s raining'

questions.hint: The apostrophe ends the string early. Use the other kind of quotes around the text.
questions.explanation: Inside double quotes, a single quote is just a character.

questions.prompt: `last` should be the final character of `word`, but this crashes with an *IndexError*. Fix it.

tests.name: last
tests.code: assert last == word[-1], 'last should be the final character of word.'
tests.message: last should be the final character.

questions.hint: If a word has 6 letters, its indexes run from 0 to 5.
questions.explanation: The last index is always one less than the length. `word[-1]` does the same job.

questions.prompt: Fill in the operator so `initials` is `AL`.
A shop shows labels like `lamp: $24`. `item` (text) and `price` (a whole number) are set. Build `label` by joining text with `+`, then print it.

tests.name: label
tests.code: assert label == item + ': $' + str(price), 'label should look like lamp: $24 — item, colon, space, dollar sign, price.'

questions.hint: Numbers must become text before joining: `str(price)`.
questions.explanation: `+` only joins strings, so the price is converted first.
An empty string has no characters; a single space has one.
